In the winter of 1978, Colorado wildlife officials moved 12 moose from Utah to North Park, a high sagebrush basin near the town of Walden. At the start of 1979, another 12 arrived from Wyoming.

Moose had never held a stable place in the state. Records from the 1850s show single bulls drifting down from Wyoming, but none started a breeding population.

This time, the animals stayed. A 1988 study found that by 1980 there were about 95 calves for every 100 cows. That is a strong sign a herd is settling in.

The reason is on the menu. Moose are browsers, and in summer more than 90 percent of their diet is willow. An adult can eat 50 to 60 pounds of willow a day. Colorado's river valleys had plenty.

The herd spread, and managers helped it along. Between 1991 and 1993, they moved 93 moose to the upper Rio Grande valley near Creede. Today, Colorado Parks and Wildlife counts roughly 3,400 moose statewide.

The first moose were seen in Rocky Mountain National Park in 1980, and park staff say moose were not resident there before the introduction. Many now live in the Kawuneeche Valley on the park's west side.

That valley is the headwaters of the Colorado River, and willows hold its wetlands together. The valley has lost 77 percent of its willow acreage since 1999. Heavy elk browsing and the decline of beavers are major causes. The park's large mammal ecologist says moose are likely making it worse. Hunting is not allowed in the park, and few large predators live there.

Since 2020, a restoration group has been working to bring the willows back. At one site, 16.5 acres of tall fencing keep moose and elk out. In the 15 years since it went up, the willows there have made a significant recovery.

Bringing moose back worked. It also added a new animal to an old system, and that system is still adjusting.

Sources : Colorado Parks and Wildlife / National Park Service.
